content: Safflower, scientifically known as Carthamus tinctorius L., is a highly branched, herbaceous annual plant that resembles a thistle. It typically grows to a height of 30 to 150 cm and is characterized by its sharp spines on the leaves. The plant produces globular flower heads, which bloom in July, and these flowers are often vibrant yellow, orange, or red in color. Each branch of the plant usually bears one to five flower heads, with each head containing 15 to 20 seeds. Safflower has a robust taproot system, which allows it to thrive in arid climates. However, it is highly vulnerable to frost damage, particularly during the period from stem elongation to maturity. Historically, safflower was cultivated primarily for its seeds, which were used to color and flavor food, as well as to produce red (carthamin) and yellow dyes. These dyes were especially important before the advent of cheaper synthetic aniline dyes. Safflower also had medicinal applications. Over the past fifty years, the primary focus of safflower cultivation has shifted to the extraction of vegetable oil from its seeds. In 2007, it was reported that genetically modified safflower had been developed to produce insulin. Safflower oil is both flavorless and colorless, with nutritional properties similar to sunflower oil. It is widely used as a cooking oil, in salad dressings, and in the production of margarine. Additionally, it is sometimes consumed as a nutritional supplement. The International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients (INCI) refers to safflower as Carthamus tinctorius. The flowers of the safflower plant are occasionally used in cooking as a less expensive alternative to saffron, earning it the nickname bastard saffron. Safflower seeds are also commonly used as a substitute for sunflower seeds in bird feeders, as squirrels tend to dislike their taste. There are two main types of safflower, each producing a different type of oil. One type is rich in monounsaturated fatty acid (oleic acid), while the other is high in polyunsaturated fatty acid (linoleic acid). The current market predominantly favors the monounsaturated variety, as it contains lower levels of saturated fats compared to oils like olive oil. Safflower oil is also utilized in painting, particularly as a substitute for linseed oil when working with white pigments, as it lacks the yellowish tint associated with linseed oil. A specific strain of safflower, known as Lana, is cultivated in the southwestern United States, particularly in Arizona and New Mexico. Safflower is one of the oldest crops cultivated by humans. Chemical analyses of ancient Egyptian textiles from the Twelfth Dynasty have revealed the presence of safflower-derived dyes. Additionally, garlands made from safflowers were discovered in the tomb of Pharaoh Tutankhamun. The Greek name for safflower appears frequently in Linear B tablets, where it is distinguished into two types: This distinction likely refers to the two usable parts of the plant: the pale seeds and the red florets. In the 19th century, safflower was also referred to as carthamine. Today, it is considered a minor crop, with an annual global production of approximately 600,000 tons across more than sixty countries. The leading producers of safflower are India, the United States, and Mexico, while Ethiopia, Kazakhstan, China, Argentina, and Australia contribute significantly to the remaining production.
